title: Ibn Battuta
hookLine: the traveler from Tangier who set out for Mecca and kept going

cards: Tangier, on the northern tip of Morocco. A young man is leaving it for Mecca, to make the pilgrimage.
In his own telling, he goes alone, with no companion and no caravan to join, and parting from his parents weighs on him, and on them. He's a student of law. He plans to come home.

Instead, the road keeps opening: Egypt, Syria, Mecca, then east and south and east again, for years, until his book reads like a map of a great stretch of the Muslim world of his time, and some lands beyond it.

teach.b: His book is called the Rihla, which simply means the journey. He didn't write it with his own pen.
Home at last in Morocco, he told his story aloud, and a court scholar named Ibn Juzayy wrote it down and polished it. So what we read is a traveler's memory, shaped by an editor.
Historians have questioned some passages, wondering whether he really reached every place he describes. That's worth knowing; the book is still a marvel. What kept him moving?
Partly the pilgrimage. Partly that a man trained in Islamic law could find work almost anywhere the law was used.

teach.h: A JUDGE, A GUEST, A WANDERER.
teach.b: In one land he serves as a judge. In another he's a guest of a sultan, then out of favor, then on the road again.
He prays in mosques he's never seen, eats at the tables of strangers, stays in lodges kept by Sufis for travelers.
The world he walks through shares a language of prayer, a law and a habit of hospitality, even when everything else changes. One verse of the Qur'an tells its hearers to go and look.

teach.h: TRAVEL IN THE LAND AND SEE.
teach.b: In Pickthall's translation: "Travel in the land and see how He originated creation." For Ibn Battuta the journey was not only distance.

It was attention: to food, to customs, to scholars, to the strangeness and sameness of people. Much of what he described was other people: what they ate, how they prayed, how they treated a stranger at the door.

how: Ibn Battuta's Rihla is read today as a travel book and a window on the Muslim world of his time, and pilgrims still set out for Mecca to perform the Hajj.

games.q: you're a young law student from Tangier. you've reached Mecca and made the pilgrimage. your plan was to go home. what do you do?
o: keep traveling, east and south and east again.
games.why: he kept going, for years, finding work as a judge and stays as a guest, and only later came home to tell it.

practice: Bring to mind somewhere near you that you've never actually been: a street you always drive past, a shop you never enter, a mosque, church or temple you've only seen from outside.

Picture walking in as Ibn Battuta might have, ready to notice what people eat, how they greet each other, what they're proud of. If you pray, ask to see it with open eyes; if you don't, simply choose the place.

wordCard.voice: Ibn Battuta. The traveler from Tangier who set out for Mecca and kept going, and whose spoken memories became the Rihla, the journey. Today's word.
